In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel therapeutic targets for chronic non-healing wounds and the role of granzyme B in the development of chronic wounds.
the development and characterization of an animal model of non-healing skin wounds in which chronic inflammation and excessive proteolytic activity are the major pathophysiological features.
the identification and characterization of the mechanisms underlying chronic wounds and the development of new therapeutic approaches to improve wound healing in this population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
granzyme B is a key player in the pathogenesis of chronic wounds.
granzyme B contributes to chronic wound persistence through its ability to degrade extracellular matrix proteins.
GzmB has an important role in the pathogenesis of impaired wound healing in AKO mice and that this may be mediated through degradation of ECM proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GzmB is a novel protease that can degrade ECM components and contributes to chronic wound closure.
GzmB has a role in the chronic wound phenotype of AKO mice, in part through degradation and/or remodeling of the ECM.
GzmB degrades ECM, and this degradation contributes to chronic inflammation and impaired healing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GzmB is an important factor in chronic wound healing and that targeting GzmB could improve healing in patients with impaired wound healing.
GzmB has a role in chronic inflammation and impaired ECM remodeling that contributes to the development of non-healing skin wounds.
granzyme B, a protein known for its role in cell death, also has a significant role in chronic inflammation and impaired ECM remodeling.
